titleStmt.title: The Digital U-Turn in Art History
titleStmt.author: Anna Näslund
Amanda Wasielewski

bibl.title: The Digital U-Turn in Art History

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The citation and theory profile of digital art history compared with mainstream art history, read as an explanation of why the field has not adopted computational methods.
span.quote: Reflecting on the historiographic trajectory of the emerging field of digital art history (DAH) versus art history more generally, we selected a sample of recent articles published between 2010-2019.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Based on our analysis, we argue that DAH methods have not been embraced by art historians more generally because of fundamental differences in the theoretical underpinnings of DAH versus the broader field of art history.

span.label: uptake of digital methods in art history
span.quote: In this article, we explore the driving factors behind art history's reticence toward the digital turn in the humanities.

span.label: text-mining-and-close-reading
span.quote: We used a mixture of methods, both digital and non-digital, to uncover the prevalence for different art-historical theories in DAH versus mainstream art history.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: DAH and mainstream art history rest on incompatible theoretical foundations, and that incompatibility - not merely missing technical skill - is what keeps art historians from taking up computational methods.
span.quote: Based on our analysis, we argue that DAH methods have not been embraced by art historians more generally because of fundamental differences in the theoretical underpinnings of DAH versus the broader field of art history.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Citing the Renaissance-focused founders of the discipline borrows their legitimacy, which is how a self-declared new field secures a place inside existing disciplinary boundaries.
span.quote: One simple explanation for this is that, as the nexus of art historical tradition, the Renaissance and its scholars confer legitimizing power, tying DAH back to some of the earliest roots of the academic discipline of art history and therefore asserting its place within disciplinary boundaries.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The image-analysis tools were built for law enforcement, warfare and science rather than for art history, so their inherited design pushes users toward superficial formal, iconographic and colour-based classification.
span.quote: Moreover, these tools favour analyses on a quite superficial level and are seldom adapted for a broader spectrum of art-historical research, since none of them were initially developed for this end, but are rather a spin-off of systems used for law enforcement, warfare and science.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because art history's primary material is images and artefacts rather than text, computational treatment is harder for it than for text-based disciplines, which partly explains its slower uptake.
span.quote: One reason for this may be that the nature of our core material – images and artefacts rather than text – makes the use of computational methods more complex for art history compared to other fields.

span.label: Digital art history is not resisted because it is new but because the theory it imports is old - formalist and iconographic methods the field spent sixty years moving away from
span.quote: Rather, they are closely tied to very particular pre-digital methods and theories of art history – very traditional ones, in fact.

span.label: Citing early art historians as if they were contemporaries strips the theories of their historical context and hides the ideological commitments built into them
span.quote: By referencing art historians like Wölfflin, Warburg and Panofsky and treating them as contemporaries, scholars ignore the ways in which historical methods reflect particular historical contexts.

span.label: The available image tools shape the questions asked, because they were built for classification and pattern-matching in other domains entirely
span.quote: Moreover, these tools favour analyses on a quite superficial level and are seldom adapted for a broader spectrum of art-historical research, since none of them were initially developed for this end, but are rather a spin-off of systems used for law enforcement, warfare and science.

span.label: Iconographic analysis and nineteenth-century scientific practice share a historical root, so the tools and the revived theory reinforce each other
span.quote: Both ideologically and technically, iconographic analysis and its focus on formal details and classification have the same historical roots as nineteenth-century scientific practices.

span.label: Frequency lists were generated over all names rather than a list the researchers supplied, specifically so the method could return names they had not thought of
span.quote: Rather than searching the material for key concepts and names, we intentionally produced frequency lists that were not limited to what we could come up with.

span.label: Counting the number of ARTICLES an author appears in, rather than total mentions, stops one heavily citing article from standing in for a field
span.quote: This means that one article with many citations of a certain author does not outweigh a corpus that does not contain any other articles that cite that author.

span.label: The prominence of Walter Benjamin as the one author shared by all three samples is left unexplained, being outside the paper's scope.
span.quote: The overlap of Benjamin between all three sets of articles – and, therefore, his singular prominence in the field of art history as represented by our sample – deserves a longer treatment that is beyond the scope of this paper.

span.label: Bias is built into the study because the researchers themselves had to decide what counted as a representative sample.
span.quote: The researcher must always define what constitutes a complete, comprehensive or representative sample, which means that bias is built in.

span.label: The computational methods are not described in technical detail in this article, being reported elsewhere.
span.quote: As this article aims to address a broad art history audience, reaching those without a technical background, we have chosen not to describe our text mining methods in technical detail here.

span.label: The mainstream comparison rests on two journals chosen to reduce interdisciplinary noise, while the authors acknowledge art history is published far more widely
span.quote: We are well aware that art history is a diverse, interdisciplinary field and this is especially true in digital humanities research.

span.label: Any computational humanities study builds in bias at the point where the sample is defined, which the authors state rather than claim to have avoided
span.quote: The researcher must always define what constitutes a complete, comprehensive or representative sample, which means that bias is built in.

span.label: Text mining alone cannot say why a name appears, which is why the study needed close reading as a second layer
span.quote: The results of these first two steps gave us a sense of the rate at which authors or theorists are mentioned in a given article in a given dataset but they did not, however, give us any sense of why they appear so often or in what context.

span.label: The technical account of the text mining is not in this paper but in two earlier ones, so the method cannot be checked from this text alone
span.quote: As this article aims to address a broad art history audience, reaching those without a technical background, we have chosen not to describe our text mining methods in technical detail here.

span.label: The single author shared across all three samples, Benjamin, is set aside as beyond scope although he is the strongest signal in the data
span.quote: The overlap of Benjamin between all three sets of articles – and, therefore, his singular prominence in the field of art history as represented by our sample – deserves a longer treatment that is beyond the scope of this paper.

span.label: text mining, a method the authors note is common in other disciplines but rare in art history, is turned back onto art-historical writing itself to study the discipline's own historiography
span.quote: we decided to use digital methods on DAH scholarship, namely text mining, to elucidate the historiographic and theoretical concerns in the uptake of computational methods in art history.

span.label: frequency lists produced over ALL names in the corpus, ordered by frequency, instead of searching the material for the key concepts and names the researchers could think of
span.quote: In short, we used this method to avoid ‘looking to confirm a theme or pattern’.

span.label: digital art history - Baca and Helmreich's wide sense: five overlapping phases beginning with digitization of archives
span.quote: The first phase is the digitization and dissemination of archives, the second is building tools for the digital humanities, the third is visualization/reconstruction/virtual reality, the fourth is experiments in alternative forms of scholarly publishing, and the fifth is algorithmically-based computational methods including machine learning and natural-language processing.

span.label: digital art history - Drucker's narrow sense: analytic computational techniques ONLY, explicitly excluding digitized repositories
span.quote: Drucker writes that ‘a clear distinction has to be made between the use of online repositories and images, which is digitized art history, and the use of analytic techniques enabled by computational technology that is the proper domain of digital art history’.

span.label: digital art history - as this paper uses it: the wider sense, adopted by explicit decision after setting out the alternatives
span.quote: For the purposes of this study, however, we define the field in the wider sense, incorporating both what Drucker terms digitized and digital art history ( Fig. 2 ).

span.label: citation frequency - number of ARTICLES an author is cited in, which is what every number here means
span.quote: After trying several alternatives, we chose to count the number of articles an author has been cited in rather than the number of times the author has been cited total, as this seems to provide a better picture of distributed frequency.

span.label: citation frequency - total mentions, the alternative that was tried and rejected because one article could then stand in for a field
span.quote: In other words, it does not matter whether an author is cited once or twenty time in one article – it will only be counted once.

span.label: novelty of DAH - as its supporters mean it: new questions and new kinds of information about art
span.quote: for example, it has been said that it will ‘enable researchers to substantially transform their methodologies and ask new types of research questions’ and that it will provide ‘entirely new types of information about art’

span.label: novelty of DAH - as its critics mean it: a symptom of new public management and the urge to quantify everything
span.quote: For the critics, it is something that has evolved as part of a new model of public management, in tandem with the contemporary urge to quantitatively evaluate every human activity.

span.label: extends → Johanna Drucker's definition of digital art history in 'Is There a "Digital" Art History?'
span.quote: For the purposes of this study, however, we define the field in the wider sense, incorporating both what Drucker terms digitized and digital art history ( Fig. 2 ).

span.label: builds-on → Paul Jaskot's question about which critical art-historical questions suit digital methods
span.quote: One answer to this call, which we believe the present study shows, is in the area of art historiography.

span.label: critiques → Manovich's argument that computational methods can approach scientific objectivity in the humanities
span.quote: However, the application of computational methodologies in the humanities is not strictly quantitative nor is it devoid of subjective considerations with regard to data collection.

span.label: critiques → the positioning of digital art history as a methodological innovation new to the discipline
span.quote: Common to both fans and critics of DAH, however, is the idea that it is a new thing.

span.label: extends → Drucker's distinction between digitized and digital art history, adopted as a distinction but not as a boundary
span.quote: While digitization projects are still often folded into DAH, Drucker’s essay shifted the meaning of the term to imply that DAH is the use of computational methods rather than use or creation of digitized archives.

span.label: supports → Jaskot's question about which critical art-historical questions are best suited to digital methods
span.quote: In a recent stock-taking of the field, Jaskot asks, ‘What are the critical questions in art history that demand and are best suited to specific digital methods?’

span.label: critiques → Bishop's Against Digital Art History, whose diagnosis the paper shares while rejecting the conclusion that computation is inherently incompatible
span.quote: While this article critiques the adherence of DAH research to the ‘old guard’ of art history, this does not mean that the use of computational tools is inherently incompatible with contemporary critical theory perspectives in the discipline.

span.label: digital art history —distinct-from→ digitized art history
span.quote: Drucker writes that ‘a clear distinction has to be made between the use of online repositories and images, which is digitized art history, and the use of analytic techniques enabled by computational technology that is the proper domain of digital art history’.

span.label: text mining —same-as→ distant reading
span.quote: We could not have ascertained the results of the text mining through close reading but nor can the ‘distant reading’ of text mining answer any deeper questions about what the presence of certain authors or theorists means for the discipline of art history.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · text mining —contrasted-with→ close reading
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span named neither method. This sentence names both and states the contrast SYMMETRICALLY - neither method could have produced the other's result, which is a stronger and more careful claim than a one-way comparison. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: Therefore we have combined quantitiative digital methods with qualitative analogue methods in this study.

span.label: meta-methodology —operationalised-as→ historiography
span.quote: This was an exercise in what might be termed meta-methodology.

span.label: formalist —part-of→ digital art history
span.quote: While surveying existing DAH literature, we have found that there is a strong focus on formal and iconographic issues in the study of art.

span.label: critical theory —distinct-from→ digital art history
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS WHICH PRE-DIGITAL TRADITION THE DIGITAL METHOD INHERITS. 'as this study shows, DAH IS CLOSELY TIED TO PARTICULAR PRE-DIGITAL METHODS AND THEORIES OF ART HISTORY, NAMELY FORMALIST AND ICONOGRAPHIC METHODS prevalent during the late nineteenth and early twentieth-century, RATHER THAN CRITICAL THEORY METHODS commonly found in more [recent work].' Digital art history is not opposed to critical theory by argument - it INHERITED A DIFFERENT ANCESTOR, and the claim is historical rather than methodological. Q-471. · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: DAH is typically positioned as something completely new to the discipline. However, as this study shows, DAH is closely tied to particular pre-digital methods and theories of art history, namely formalist and iconographic methods prevalent during the late nineteenth and early twentieth-century, rather than critical theory methods commonly found in more recent art-historical scholarship.

span.label: Heinrich Wölfflin —is-a→ formalist
span.quote: Although Wölfflin is considered one of the founding fathers of art history alongside Warburg and Panofsky, his methods and theory have largely disappeared in art historical scholarship.

span.label: Erwin Panofsky —is-a→ iconographic
span.quote: In particular, we have frequently seen references to the theories and methods popular among early art historians like Heinrich Wölfflin, Aby Warburg and Erwin Panofsky, which have fallen somewhat out of favour in recent art historical research.

span.label: Walter Benjamin —part-of→ digital art history
span.quote: We found that the only author shared between the three groups of articles was Walter Benjamin.

span.label: exploratory data analysis —same-as→ unsupervised learning
span.quote: Lev Manovich describes the concept of drawing unknown patterns from a given set of data as ‘exploratory data analysis’ or ‘unsupervised learning’, borrowing terminology from machine learning.

span.label: pattern recognition —causes→ iconographic
span.quote: The current digital image analysis tools typically lend themselves to iconographic, pattern recognition and categorizations based on form or colour.

span.label: digital art history —distinct-from→ canon
span.quote: For example, DAH often fails to acknowledge the ways in which art-historical study has expanded beyond western art and how scholars continue to rethink the traditional canon of art history.

span.label: network analysis —contrasted-with→ text mining
span.quote: More recently, Paul Jaskot proposed four areas where digital tools may be useful for art historians: digital storytelling, text-based analysis, network analysis and spatial analysis.

span.label: historiography —part-of→ digital art history
span.quote: One answer to this call, which we believe the present study shows, is in the area of art historiography.

span.label: text mining —contrasted-with→ close reading
span.note: strength of the relation: 1 — RE-GROUNDS n-slund2021-the-digital-u-turn-in-art-history[2]: the relation was always stated, the endpoint names were not in the span.
span.quote: We could not have ascertained the results of the text mining through close reading but nor can the ‘distant reading’ of text mining answer any deeper questions

span.label: frequency count
span.quote: Rather than searching the material for key concepts and names, we intentionally produced frequency lists that were not limited to what we could come up with.

span.label: text mining (word-frequency analysis in R)
span.quote: We chose to use a standard text mining method using the text mining (tm package) in R.

span.label: Across the three article corpora, Walter Benjamin was the single author cited in common by all three.
span.quote: We found that the only author shared between the three groups of articles was Walter Benjamin.

span.label: Art Journal, the contemporary-art journal one might expect to align with digital practice, shares no frequently cited author with the DAH corpus other than Benjamin.
span.quote: As shown in the Venn diagram in Fig. 3 , Art Journal had no overlap of authors with DAH apart from Benjamin.

span.label: The two mainstream art-history journals resemble each other far more than either resembles DAH, and Art Journal is the more distant of the two from DAH.
span.quote: Overall, the list of authors frequently cited in Art Journal and DAH differed more than DAH and Art History , while Art Journal and Art History had far more in common with each other.

span.label: Besides Benjamin, only Erwin Panofsky, Aby Warburg and Hans Belting are shared between the Art History and DAH citation lists.
span.quote: We found only three overlapping authors between Art History and DAH besides Benjamin: Erwin Panofsky, Aby Warburg and Hans Belting.

span.label: Heinrich Wolfflin, largely abandoned in mainstream art-historical scholarship, is frequently cited in DAH literature and appears in neither mainstream journal sample.
span.quote: He is not frequently cited in either our Art History or Art Journal sample, but his name often appears in DAH literature ( Fig. 4 ).

span.label: Close reading showed that shared citation counts hide opposite uses: DAH cites Panofsky as if his iconology settled the question until computers arrived, whereas Art History places him in dialogue with, and under criticism from, later theory.
span.quote: DAH literature, on the other hand, seems to suggest through its omission of other similar types of scholarship or critique of Panofsky that his work was the final word on the subject – until digitization came along.

span.label: Studies using computational methods turn out not to be qualitatively different from analogue art history; they are bound to a specific and very traditional set of pre-digital formalist and iconographic methods.
span.quote: Rather, they are closely tied to very particular pre-digital methods and theories of art history – very traditional ones, in fact.

span.label: By citing Wolfflin, Warburg and Panofsky as if they were contemporaries, DAH strips those methods of their historical context and downplays sixty years of critique that reshaped the discipline.
span.quote: In other words, DAH appears to de-historicize art historical theories and methods.

span.label: Colour-based digital analyses such as Hristova's remapping of Warburg's panel 45 rest on an unexamined assumption that digital reproductions faithfully preserve the artwork's brightness, hue and saturation.
span.quote: A critical factor left unremarked in this article, which is also a significant barrier in Manovich’s methodology as generally applied, is the assumption that digital images of artworks are ‘true’ to the brightness, hue and saturation of the artworks themselves.

span.label: only one author, Walter Benjamin, is shared across all three samples
span.quote: We found that the only author shared between the three groups of articles was Walter Benjamin.

span.label: besides Benjamin, digital art history shares only three authors with Art History and none with Art Journal
span.quote: As shown in the Venn diagram in Fig. 3 , Art Journal had no overlap of authors with DAH apart from Benjamin.

span.label: Wölfflin is prominent in digital art history and largely absent from both mainstream journals
span.quote: He is not frequently cited in either our Art History or Art Journal sample, but his name often appears in DAH literature ( Fig. 4 ).

span.label: the two mainstream journals resemble each other more than either resembles digital art history
span.quote: Overall, the list of authors frequently cited in Art Journal and DAH differed more than DAH and Art History , while Art Journal and Art History had far more in common with each other.

span.label: computational art history is not qualitatively different from analogue art history - it is tied to a particular old strand of it
span.quote: What our meta-methodology, using mixed methods for a historiographical study of this emerging field shows, however, is that studies using computational methods are not qualitatively different from analogue art history.

span.label: Benjamin is cited differently in the two literatures - named in DAH, worked with elsewhere
span.quote: However, broadly speaking, citations of Benjamin in DAH typically mention his famous essay without engaging in further analysis.

span.label: digital art history (DAH), defined broadly for this study
span.term: digital art history (DAH), defined broadly for this study
span.quote: For the purposes of this study, however, we define the field in the wider sense, incorporating both what Drucker terms digitized and digital art history ( Fig. 2 ).

span.label: digitized art history versus digital art history (Drucker's distinction)
span.term: digitized art history versus digital art history (Drucker's distinction)
span.quote: Drucker writes that ‘a clear distinction has to be made between the use of online repositories and images, which is digitized art history, and the use of analytic techniques enabled by computational technology that is the proper domain of digital art history’.

span.label: meta-methodology
span.quote: This was an exercise in what might be termed meta-methodology.

span.label: text mining
span.quote: Simply put, this text mining consisted of automatically collecting all the words in a text and analyzing them quantitatively for patterns.

span.label: Kunstgeschichte ohne Namen (art history without names)
span.term: Kunstgeschichte ohne Namen (art history without names)
span.quote: proponents of quantitative analysis for large digital images collections have strong affinities with Wölfflin, whose concept of ‘Kunstgeschichte ohne Namen’ (art history without names) is a model and a precursor to contemporary formalist digital methodologies.

span.label: digitized art history
span.quote: a clear distinction has to be made between the use of online repositories and images, which is digitized art history, and the use of analytic techniques enabled by computational technology that is the proper domain of digital art history

span.label: exploratory data analysis
span.quote: Lev Manovich describes the concept of drawing unknown patterns from a given set of data as ‘exploratory data analysis’ or ‘unsupervised learning’, borrowing terminology from machine learning.

span.label: meta-methodology
span.quote: In order to investigate these differences, we decided to use digital methods on DAH scholarship, namely text mining, to elucidate the historiographic and theoretical concerns in the uptake of computational methods in art history.

span.label: article corpus / journal of publication (DAH vs Art History vs Art Journal)
span.term: article corpus / journal of publication (DAH vs Art History vs Art Journal)
span.quote: In order to compare the citations and topics in DAH with other research in the field of art history, we created a corpus of all articles published in the journals Art History and Art Journal between 2010 and 2019.

span.label: number of articles in which an author is cited (distributed citation frequency)
span.term: number of articles in which an author is cited (distributed citation frequency)
span.quote: After trying several alternatives, we chose to count the number of articles an author has been cited in rather than the number of times the author has been cited total, as this seems to provide a better picture of distributed frequency.

span.label: publication venue (DAH, Art History, Art Journal)
span.term: publication venue (DAH, Art History, Art Journal)
span.quote: In order to compare the citations and topics in DAH with other research in the field of art history, we created a corpus of all articles published in the journals Art History and Art Journal between 2010 and 2019.

span.label: number of articles an author is cited in
span.term: number of articles an author is cited in
span.quote: After trying several alternatives, we chose to count the number of articles an author has been cited in rather than the number of times the author has been cited total, as this seems to provide a better picture of distributed frequency.

span.label: how a cited author is used in the body text
span.term: how a cited author is used in the body text
span.quote: Our next step was, therefore, to look for where these names are referenced in the body text of articles.

span.label: 61 — articles in the combined digital-art-history corpus (two Visual Resources special issues plus DAHJ 2015-2019)
span.quote: The combined DAH corpus contained 61 articles in total.

span.label: 373 / 215 — articles drawn from Art History and from Art Journal for the 2010-2019 comparison corpora
span.quote: The total number of articles from Art History was 373 and from Art Journal 215.

span.label: thirty-five — number of top cited scholars extracted per corpus and compared in the Venn diagram
span.quote: Through text mining, we were able to obtain a list of the top thirty-five scholars cited in Art History , Art Journal and our DAH sample from the last ten years.

span.label: 100 — length of the most-frequent-word list produced for each dataset after stopword removal
span.quote: We used two different techniques to determine the top 100 most frequently mentioned words in each datasets, minus stopwords.

span.label: top thirty-five scholars — the size of the citation list compared across the three samples
span.quote: Through text mining, we were able to obtain a list of the top thirty-five scholars cited in Art History , Art Journal and our DAH sample from the last ten years.

span.label: 2010 and 2019 — the decade of mainstream art history sampled
span.quote: In order to compare the citations and topics in DAH with other research in the field of art history, we created a corpus of all articles published in the journals Art History and Art Journal between 2010 and 2019.

span.label: three overlapping authors — the entire shared ground between DAH and Art History besides Benjamin
span.quote: We found only three overlapping authors between Art History and DAH besides Benjamin: Erwin Panofsky, Aby Warburg and Hans Belting.

span.label: five ‘roughly chronological’ and overlapping phases — the structure of the wide definition of the field
span.quote: The editors of the issue, Murtha Baca and Anne Helmreich, identify five ‘roughly chronological’ and overlapping phases of development.
